Speculative decoding accelerates inference by having a small draft model propose token continuations that a large target model then accepts or rejects in parallel — the speedup depends entirely on the draft acceptance rate, which is highest when the two models assign similar probability distributions over next tokens. The central question here is: what happens to that acceptance rate when the target model has been fine-tuned on a specialized domain (medical notes, legal text, code in a niche language) while the draft model remains anchored to its general pretraining distribution? The expert worry that beginners miss is that acceptance rate degradation isn't uniform or predictable — it clusters on exactly the tokens that matter most in the fine-tuned domain: domain-specific terminology, stylistic conventions, and distributional quirks the fine-tune introduced precisely because the base model got them wrong. A beginner looks at a 10% drop in average acceptance rate and calls it a minor regression; an expert recognizes that the rejected tokens are disproportionately the high-stakes, low-entropy predictions where the target model is most confidently diverging from the draft — meaning you're not just losing speed, you're doing the most expensive re-evaluation on the most semantically loaded positions. Compounding this, the draft model's errors in the fine-tuned domain often cascade: a wrong token early in a speculated sequence forces rejection of subsequent tokens that would have been accepted under the correct prefix, so the effective alignment drift is worse than a token-level mismatch rate suggests.

The non-obvious tradeoff is that the draft model's job is not to be good at the task — it's to be a cheap approximator of the target model's distribution, which means fine-tuning the draft model on domain data can actually hurt if it makes the draft better than the target on certain sub-distributions, increasing rejection on those positions. Joint fine-tuning (training draft and target together with a shared objective) is the cleanest theoretical solution and is what Medusa and Eagle-2 gesture toward by training draft heads directly on the target model's hidden states — but this requires access to the target model's internals during fine-tuning, which breaks down in the common deployment scenario where the target is a black-box API or a separately owned checkpoint. Fine-tuning the draft separately afterward is tractable but introduces a moving-target problem: you're distilling from a distribution you're approximating with finite samples, and if the fine-tuning domain is small (say, a 50k-example clinical dataset), the draft may overfit to surface features of that domain rather than tracking the target's actual conditional distribution. Replacing the draft entirely with a smaller model from the same fine-tuning lineage (e.g., using Llama-3-8B as draft for Llama-3-70B fine-tuned on legal text, then swapping to a fine-tuned Llama-3-1B draft) is often the most practical path and is implicitly what teams at Together AI and Fireworks have converged on for production speculative decoding. The key number that crystallizes the tradeoff: draft fine-tuning on domain data typically recovers 60–80% of the acceptance rate lost to distribution shift, but the remaining 20–40% gap often requires architectural co-design — meaning there's a hard floor on what post-hoc draft adaptation can achieve without touching the target model's training.

Consider fine-tuning a target model on a small, noisy clinical dataset where the "correct" output for a given context is genuinely ambiguous — multiple valid ICD-10 codes, paraphrased diagnoses, varied physician note styles — and the fine-tuning signal is too weak to sharpen the target's distribution, instead spreading probability mass more diffusely across plausible continuations. In this scenario, the target's distribution after fine-tuning becomes easier for the draft to satisfy: the acceptance criterion in standard speculative decoding (DejaVu, the original Chen et al. 2023 formulation) accepts a draft token whenever the target's probability for that token exceeds the draft's, so a flatter target distribution mechanically raises acceptance rate even though the draft hasn't moved at all. This is not hypothetical — it's a known failure mode analogous to what Leviathan et al. flagged about acceptance rate being a function of the ratio of distributions, not their absolute quality, meaning a poorly calibrated or oversmoothed target can appear to "agree" with the draft more often while actually producing worse outputs. The diagnostic implication is severe: acceptance rate conflates two completely different causal stories — genuine draft-target alignment versus target entropy inflation — and you cannot distinguish them from acceptance rate alone without also tracking the target's per-token entropy or perplexity on a held-out reference set. A system optimized to maximize acceptance rate could in principle regularize the target toward higher entropy during fine-tuning and achieve near-perfect acceptance while destroying task performance, which means acceptance rate as a primary KPI creates a Goodhart's law failure mode that production teams using speculative decoding for fine-tuned models should treat as a live risk.

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-1681)
response:
The minimally sufficient suite has three components: acceptance rate (to catch obvious regressions), mean target entropy at accepted positions (to detect the inflation pathology), and task-level output quality on a domain benchmark (to anchor both to what actually matters) — and the three together take maybe 200 lines of instrumentation but catch qualitatively different failure modes that none catches alone. If forced to instrument only one thing, the strongest candidate is the Jensen-Shannon divergence between the draft and target distributions at each position, averaged over a representative domain sample — JSD is bounded in [0, 1], symmetric, defined even when distributions have non-overlapping support, and crucially it moves in opposite directions for the two failure modes: genuine alignment pushes JSD down, while target entropy inflation leaves JSD largely unchanged or increases it (because spreading the target's mass doesn't make it closer to the draft's concentrated prediction, it just makes the ratio criterion easier to satisfy). This is a sharper signal than KL divergence, which Stern et al. and the Speculative Decoding literature have used implicitly, because KL is asymmetric and can be gamed by exactly the entropy-inflation pathology — a diffuse target has low KL against almost anything. The practical obstacle is that computing full-vocabulary JSD requires materializing both distributions at each token position, which is expensive if the draft and target live on different hardware or if the target is partially black-box; a cheap approximation is to compute JSD only over the top-K tokens (K=50 or K=100 captures >95% of probability mass for typical language model distributions), reducing it to a tractable sparse operation. What this suite still doesn't tell you is where in the sequence the misalignment is concentrated — a position-weighted JSD profile, sorted by token semantic category, would be the next instrumentation layer worth adding for any team doing serious domain-adapted speculative decoding in production.

Using JSD as a distillation loss is theoretically attractive because it's symmetric — it penalizes the draft equally for missing mass the target places on a token and for placing mass on tokens the target ignores — but this symmetry is precisely what breaks it as a training objective for speculative decoding, because the acceptance criterion only cares about one direction: whether the draft underestimates the target's probability on the proposed token. Minimizing JSD pushes the draft to also reduce probability on tokens the target has deprioritized, which wastes model capacity on a constraint the acceptance mechanism never checks and can actively hurt the draft's ability to make sharp, confident proposals — a draft that has been symmetrically regularized toward the target's full distribution will have higher entropy and propose less greedily, reducing the expected length of accepted sequences. Standard forward-KL distillation (cross-entropy from target to draft) is mean-seeking and has its own pathology — it forces the draft to cover all modes of the target, spreading mass across low-probability tokens — but reverse-KL, which is what you implicitly optimize when the draft proposes and the target rejects, is mode-seeking and better matches the operational dynamic of speculative decoding, a point made concrete in the DistillSpec paper (Zhou et al., 2023) which showed reverse-KL distillation outperforming forward-KL for draft training by 10-15% in acceptance rate on standard benchmarks. The deeper problem with any distribution-matching loss, JSD included, is that it treats all token positions equally during training, whereas the acceptance rate impact of misalignment is highly position-dependent — a single misaligned token at position one of a speculative window kills the entire speculated suffix, so a loss that weights early positions in the draft window more heavily would better reflect the actual cost structure, and no standard distillation objective does this without custom modification. The practical upshot is that JSD is best kept as a diagnostic and regularizer rather than a primary loss, and the most principled current approach is reverse-KL as the main objective with position-weighted sampling during draft fine-tuning — though this remains an open engineering problem with no widely adopted clean solution as of mid-2025.

Yes, and the cleanest framing is to treat the draft model as a conditional policy that outputs not just a token proposal but a speculation length — proposing 4 tokens when confident, 1 when uncertain, and 0 (deferring immediately to the target) when it detects it's in a distribution region where it systematically loses. This is essentially what SpecTr and later Adaptive Speculation (Miao et al., 2024) explore: rather than a fixed speculation horizon, the draft learns a stopping criterion, though current implementations base this on shallow signals like draft logit entropy rather than an explicit learned rejection-probability estimator. The architectural change required for a genuinely uncertainty-conditioned draft is a lightweight auxiliary head trained to predict acceptance probability for each proposed token — a binary classifier that takes the draft's hidden state and outputs p(accept), trained on logged accept/reject decisions from the target during a calibration phase. The training challenge is that this creates a distribution shift loop: the classifier is trained on historical rejection patterns, but deploying a conservative draft changes the distribution of contexts the target sees, which changes rejection patterns, requiring periodic re-calibration — a non-stationary learning problem that standard offline distillation doesn't handle. The most practical near-term realization is probably a learned dynamic speculation length that uses the draft's own token-level entropy as a proxy for p(accept), with a threshold tuned per domain — empirically, draft entropy above roughly 2.5-3.0 nats correlates strongly with rejection in domain-shifted settings, giving you a cheap gating signal without a separate classifier head. The deeper architectural question is whether the draft should share a prefix encoder with the target (as in Eagle's feature-level distillation) so that its uncertainty estimates are computed in the same representational space as the acceptance decision — without that, the draft's self-assessed confidence and the target's actual rejection probability are measuring fundamentally different things.

A non-obvious fact: alignment drift under domain shift is not monotone in the degree of domain specialization — there exists a regime where moderate fine-tuning of the target increases draft acceptance rate relative to the base target, because fine-tuning on a focused domain reduces the target's uncertainty at positions where the base model was hedging, and if the draft's pretraining corpus happened to contain even a small amount of that domain, the draft's modal predictions now align better with a sharper target than they did with a diffuse base model. This non-monotonicity was implicitly observable in experiments from the DistillSpec paper and in ablations from the Medusa team, where acceptance rates on coding benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP) after code-focused fine-tuning of the target were sometimes higher than on the base model, even with an unchanged general-purpose draft — the fine-tuning sharpened the target onto exactly the tokens the draft was already confidently predicting from code seen during pretraining. The implication is that "distribution shift" is not a single scalar quantity but a vector: shift in vocabulary frequency, shift in syntactic patterns, shift in output length distribution, and shift in entropy profile all move semi-independently, and a draft can be well-aligned on some axes while severely misaligned on others. This means the standard advice to always fine-tune the draft when you fine-tune the target is wrong in a precise sense: if the fine-tuning domain is well-represented in the draft's pretraining corpus, draft fine-tuning can introduce new misalignment by moving the draft away from a pretraining distribution that was already well-matched to the newly sharpened target. The practical diagnostic consequence is that you should always measure post-fine-tuning acceptance rate before deciding whether to adapt the draft — the answer may be "do nothing," and teams that automatically trigger draft fine-tuning pipelines on every target update are potentially degrading their own systems.
